extracted.intended_audience: employers, labor lawyers, labor regulators, and other stakeholders assessing worker classification under the FLSA (Department of Labor rulemaking commenters)
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory guidance from the Department of Labor interpreting the FLSA economic-reality test for distinguishing employees from independent contractors, describing the relevant factors and how courts and the Department evaluate them in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanence of the relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: Permanence (including length and longevity of the relationship) is a factor in the economic reality test; long tenure or repeatedly renewed engagements supports employee status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automatic contract renewal and long continuous service are evidence of substantial permanence (e.g., one-year contracts that were routinely renewed indicated employee status). The Department considered whether to articulate this factor as “permanence and exclusivity of the working relationship” but treats exclusivity separately as it may inform permanence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusivity of the working relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the worker works primarily or exclusively for the potential employer can be probative of economic dependence and thus employee status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusivity may inform both the permanence and control factors. Courts have found that primarily/exclusively working for one employer for several years supports employee status, but non-exclusivity does not automatically preclude employee status (employees may work for more than one employer). The Department considers exclusivity as relevant under multiple factors where it contributes to the totality of circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control (degree of employer control over how work is performed)
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which the alleged employer has the right to control the manner in which the work is performed is a central factor in the economic reality analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control includes whether the employer supervises, disciplines, sets schedules, dictates how tasks are performed, sets prices or compensation, or can fire the worker. The Department stresses a qualitative, totality-of-the-circumstances analysis and rejects using the listed indicia as a mechanical checklist or arithmetic tally. Courts have found that substantial control over meaningful economic aspects of the work indicates employee status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervision and monitoring (including technological monitoring)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of meaningful supervision and monitoring—whether in-person or via technological systems—may indicate employee status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include follow-alongs, requiring workers to call supervisors after stops, route-monitoring screens, logging in/out on devices, and electronic visitor verification (EVV) systems. Even where direct, day-to-day supervision is limited, use of monitoring systems or reserved rights to supervise can weigh in favor of employee status. At the same time, monitoring solely to ensure product integrity or regulatory compliance may be less probative (see separate guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Schedule flexibility and ability to set hours
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a worker sets their own hours, selects shifts, can accept/reject work, or is otherwise free to determine schedule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schedule flexibility can weigh toward independent contractor status (courts have noted that setting one's own hours is evidence of independence). However, flexibility alone is not dispositive—courts often treat it as a ‘narrow choice’ when other indicia of control or lack of opportunity for profit exist. Practical constraints (e.g., required hours, coordination needs) can negate the significance of nominal schedule flexibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity for profit or loss / ability to exercise managerial skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the worker can affect his/her own profits or losses through managerial skill, e.g., by selecting jobs, negotiating prices, hiring help, or controlling costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ability to select more favorable jobs/loads, hire others, control distribution territories, or otherwise influence revenue and expenses weighs toward independent contractor status. Conversely, flat-rate pay that forecloses profit based on performance points toward employee status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who sets prices / ability to negotiate compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the employer sets the price or pay rate for the worker's services or the worker can negotiate or control pricing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An employer setting prices or fees (for example, for private dances, deliveries, or products sold) has been treated as evidence of pervasive control pointing to employee status. The mere ability to accept or reject an offered rate does not equal bargaining power to negotiate a rate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractual terms and written agreements (e.g., non-compete, independent-contractor agreement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence and content of written agreements, such as non-compete clauses or independent-contractor agreements, can be evidence but are not determinative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A covenant-not-to-compete or similar contractual restraints can support a finding of employee status, but such provisions do not automatically negate independent-contractor classification. Conversely, an agreement lacking a covenant-not-to-compete and allowing work for others can support independent-contractor status. The Department will not opine on every discrete contractual provision in a final rule and cautions against treating contract language as dispositive without examining the facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic renewal and contract duration
rubrics_metrics.description: Automatic renewal of contracts and the apparent indefinite duration of the relationship bear on permanence and may indicate employee status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have noted that regular automatic renewals of one-year contracts suggest substantial permanence of the relationship, which weighs in favor of employee classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to hire helpers / delegation of work
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the worker has the right to hire others or delegate work as part of exercising independent business judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ability to hire others and run a business-like operation (including managing assistants or subcontractors) is an indicium of independent contractor status, whereas lack of such rights is consistent with employee status. Courts examine this right in the context of other factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration into the principal's business (integral part)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the services rendered are an integral part of the potential employer's business operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative history and case law identify integrality of services as relevant: services that are integral to the principal’s business suggest an employment relationship. This is considered alongside the worker's initiative and other factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer's reserved right to supervise or perform oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the employer retains the right to supervise, discipline, or otherwise oversee workers—even if it exercises that right only occasionally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reservation of supervisory rights (for example, the employer's reserved right to perform in-person supervision) is relevant to the economic reality analysis and can indicate employee status even if day-to-day supervision is not continuously exercised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control exercised to comply with regulatory or safety obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Control that an employer asserts it exercises solely to satisfy regulatory, safety, or customer-protection obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department notes that requiring certain practices (e.g., hard hats on a construction site) may be less probative of control indicative of employment, but such regulatory- or safety-motivated control can nonetheless be considered as part of the totality of circumstances and, in some cases, courts have still concluded worker status is employee despite such explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple income sources / working for multiple employers
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a worker has multiple sources of income or works for multiple employers does not, by itself, negate economic dependence on a particular employer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department and courts reject conflating multiple income sources with lack of economic dependence. The proper inquiry is dependence-for-work (whether a worker is economically dependent on a particular business for continued employment), not mere dependence-for-income. It is possible to be an employee in one line of work and an independent contractor in another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical ability to work for others (versus contractual allowance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a worker can actually work for other employers in practice—even if a contract formally allows it—is relevant to control and opportunity-for-profit analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have found that practical constraints (e.g., required hours, scheduling that makes it impossible to provide services to others) can show that, notwithstanding contractual permission, the worker is effectively exclusive to one employer and that control favors employee status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-dispositive, totality-of-the-circumstances approach
rubrics_metrics.description: No single factor is dispositive; the employment relationship determination depends on qualitative, holistic consideration of all relevant facts and circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department emphasizes that the economic reality inquiry examines multiple indicia (control, permanence, opportunity for profit/loss, initiative, integrality, etc.) and avoids treating the list of considerations as a simple checklist or arithmetic tally. Courts have repeatedly held that relative weight of each factor depends on the facts of the case.
